Donald Trump just proposed repealing the 'death tax.' Here's why that's a scam.

As a lowly young worker (ran a department/supervised at night) in a grocery store business, I got to watch as myself and 600+ middle to lower class people got laid off due to a "death tax"/ "estate tax" fiasco.

"Let's GET those evil rich people!", we cry. "They made their money on our backs!"

And then, the owner of the place you work at dies suddenly. He is sole owner of the company (kids had minority shares.) He was working on an ESOP plan, but it hadn't been finalized. His estate plan was unfinished due to the ESOP situation. He had lived in the same house since 1950, over 49 years. Nice neighborhood, about a 1800 square foot brick 2 story. He got a new Cadillac every 5 years. No boat, no big African safaris, no orgies of wine and food.

IRS comes in, does an inventory. Every box of cereal, every can of soup is calculated (AT RETAIL) and added to the guy's estate. Family is told, "You OWE US $7 million." The estate outside of the company's assets amounted to roughly $450,000. SO, they had $450,000 of assets, and a $7 million tax bill. So, they sold the company.

We all got laid off. We would "allowed" to be re-interviewed. Managers were not allowed to re-interview at same level. Could apply for asst. manager positions. Perks no longer provided - 1.5x pay on Sundays, free prescriptions, no health care co-pay, vacations restarted at 2 weeks, and none in first year. 401(k) disbanded.

Where are the lost wages, lost jobs, missed vacations, lost seniority, lost pension, etc. calculated in these statistics? Where are the tens (or hundreds) of millions spent on estate lawyers included in these figures? What is the lost productivity of that money that could be plowed into the business for growth, new jobs, etc. instead of for estate planning, asset hiding, financial shenanigans, etc. accounted for in the data? or does real-world effects of these policies not look good on paper, so are excluded? How about the loss of small businesses to next generations, or the competitive advantage public companies have over private ones in terms of estate planning? How many small businesses have sold out to giant conglomerates because the giant conglomerates don't have to pay estate taxes directly?

End the estate tax. The money was taxed once already. Let it be. Let small business owners pass along their businesses to their kids. Level the playing field for small companies against the giant publicly traded companies. Go small business, BOO Estate taxes.

Where are you getting your math from?
Even at today's rates of 40% over $5 million, the estate would only have to be valued at $22.5 (40% of $17,5 million = $7 million). And having 6 grocery stores, it doesn't take long to get to that value, when inventory is included. The company had revenues of around $1.2 million/ week on average - roughly $60 million/year in sales. You generally turned your inventory 3-5 times a year, so at any given time, you were holding about $12-20 million in INVENTORY alone. Add to that, delivery trucks, equipment assets (bakery ovens, smokehouse, coolers, freezers, etc.), building assets (6 stores LHI's + warehouse), and Bob's your uncle. A $30 million valuation is not that difficult.

As for single ownership, the owner would defer his shareholder equity back into investment in the business (borrowing from himself), but since he was the creditor as well as the debtor, these offset, leaving asset value = company value.

Running a business from 1947 until 1998, making it from a single store into a $30+ million business isn't exactly rich person status.
